name: Prior Art and Clearance Searching
title: Prior Art and Clearance Searching
answer: Prior art and clearance searching is the process of identifying existing patents, published applications, non-patent literature, and registered or common law trademarks that could affect the validity of a new filing or the freedom to use a proposed mark or product. It covers patentability searches, freedom to operate searches, invalidity searches, and trademark clearance searches across classes and jurisdictions. The goal is to give an inventor, brand owner, or attorney a reliable picture of what already exists before money is spent on prosecution or launch.

sections.body: Prior art and clearance searching is the process of identifying existing patents, published applications, non-patent literature, and registered or common law trademarks that could affect the validity of a new filing or the freedom to use a proposed mark or product. It covers patentability searches, freedom to operate searches, invalidity searches, and trademark clearance searches across classes and jurisdictions. The goal is to give an inventor, brand owner, or attorney a reliable picture of what already exists before money is spent on prosecution or launch.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on commercial patent and trademark databases, public registries such as those of the USPTO, WIPO, and EUIPO, and internal document collections. Search platforms increasingly add machine learning ranking, semantic query expansion, and automated classification to surface relevant records from millions of documents. A typical setup combines a primary database with citation networks, legal status data, and file wrapper or office action histories.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Searchers begin by breaking an invention or mark into concepts, classes, keywords, synonyms, and relevant Cooperative Patent Classification or Nice Classification codes. They run iterative queries, review result sets, and use citation chaining and examiner citations to find additional references. AI tools can rank results by similarity, suggest alternative terms, and cluster documents, but a qualified attorney or search professional still reviews the output for relevance and materiality.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Clearance and prior art work carries legal risk because a missed reference can lead to rejection, opposition, cancellation, or infringement claims. The site's tracking of 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, shows how clearance failures become disputes. Search reports should record the databases, date ranges, query strings, and classification codes used so the scope and limits of the search are clear. No search is exhaustive, and a negative result is only as strong as the sources and methods behind it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward continuous monitoring rather than one-off searches, with alerts tied to new publications, applications, and trademark filings. Generative AI is being tested for summarising large result sets and drafting search strategies, though human verification remains essential. As AI-generated prior art and AI-assisted inventions grow, searchers will need clearer rules on what counts as a public disclosure and how to attribute machine contributions.
